n: Chronicles was written after the Exile for a community with no king. It retells Samuel and Kings with the dark episodes (Bethsabee, Absalom) left out, and gives the promise to David an even longer horizon: 'I will settle him in my house and in my kingdom for ever'.

At the dedication of the Temple God promises that repentance can reverse drought, locusts and plague. The verse became a favourite of national prayer movements. In context it belongs to Solomon's Temple and Israel's covenant; the Chronicler wrote it for exiles wondering whether return was still possible.

A pagan Persian king ends the Babylonian exile, and Isaiah 45 had already called him the Lord's 'anointed'. The decree (also known from the Cyrus Cylinder) let subject peoples return and rebuild their temples. Ezra and Nehemiah tell the slow, contested rebuilding of Jerusalem.

Ezra reads the Torah from dawn to noon while Levites 'explained the sense' — the origin of the synagogue habit of reading and homily, and so of the Christian liturgy of the Word. The people weep, then are told to feast: 'the joy of the Lord is our strength'.

The travelling companion 'Azarias' turns out to be Raphael, 'one of the seven who stand before the Lord'. Tobit's teaching on almsgiving, burial of the dead and prayer made it a favourite of the early Church; Protestant Bibles place it among the Apocrypha. The dog that follows Tobias is one of the Bible's few pets.

A widow of Bethulia enters the enemy camp, charms the Assyrian general and cuts off his head with his own sword. Painters from Caravaggio to Artemisia Gentileschi made it their subject. The book is a theological novel — its geography and history are deliberately impossible — about faith that acts.

Mardochai's message to Queen Esther: if she keeps silent, deliverance will come from elsewhere, but perhaps she was made queen for this very moment. The Hebrew Esther never mentions God; the Greek additions (Vulgate chapters 10–16) supply the prayers the Hebrew leaves out.

'Satan' here is a title — 'the accuser', a prosecuting angel among 'the sons of God' — not yet the devil of later theology. His wager: does Job serve God for nothing? The whole book tests whether love of God can survive when every reward is stripped away.

t: 'The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away'
n: Job's first response to losing everything is worship. 'Naked came I out of my mother's womb, and naked shall I return' is recited at Jewish funerals and quoted at Christian ones. Note that the book does not leave him there — thirty chapters of protest follow.

t: Job curses the day of his birth
n: After seven days of silence with his friends, Job speaks — and the patient Job of chapters 1–2 vanishes. From here to chapter 37 the book is poetry: three cycles of speeches in which the friends defend God's justice and Job demands a hearing. The book honours the protest more than the defence.

Job's cry of hope in the middle of despair. Jerome's Latin — 'in the last day I shall rise out of the earth, and in my flesh I shall see my God' — reads it as a prophecy of resurrection, and Handel set it in Messiah. The Hebrew is harder and more ambiguous; Job wants a vindicator, and gets one in chapter 42.

t: God answers out of the whirlwind
n: God does not explain Job's suffering. Instead he asks seventy questions about creation: 'Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?' The answer to the problem of evil offered here is not an argument but an encounter — and Job says it is enough (42:5).

t: God sides with Job against the friends
n: The twist: God says the friends, who defended him, 'have not spoken the thing that is right before me, as my servant Job hath'. Honest anger at God is closer to him than tidy theology. Job must pray for his comforters, and his fortunes are restored double.

Psalm 1 was placed first as the entrance to the whole Psalter: two ways, the just and the wicked, and a tree planted by running waters. 'Meditate' (meditabitur) meant murmuring the text aloud — how the psalms were always meant to be used.

t: 'Thou art my son, this day have I begotten thee'
n: A coronation psalm for the kings of Judah becomes the New Testament's favourite text about Jesus: quoted at his baptism and transfiguration, in Acts 13 and three times in Hebrews. Vulgate numbering: this is Psalm 2 in all traditions.

t: 'What is man, that thou art mindful of him?'
n: Awe at the night sky turns to awe at human dignity: 'a little less than the angels' (the Hebrew says 'than God'). Hebrews 2 applies it to Christ, crowned after being made lower. Neil Armstrong's crewmate Buzz Aldrin read this psalm on the moon.

t: 'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?'
n: Vulgate Psalm 21 is Psalm 22 in Hebrew and most English Bibles. Jesus quoted its first line from the cross; the psalm goes on to describe pierced hands and feet, mocking, and lots cast for clothing, then turns into praise. Read all of it to hear what Jesus was praying.

t: 'The Lord ruleth me' — the shepherd psalm
n: Vulgate Psalm 22 is the beloved Psalm 23 of the Hebrew numbering. Jerome's Dominus regit me ('the Lord rules me') is the Douay's odd 'ruleth'; the Hebrew is 'the Lord is my shepherd'. Green pastures, still waters, the valley of the shadow of death, a table and an overflowing cup.

Psalm 50 (51 in Hebrew numbering): David's repentance after Nathan's rebuke. 'Create a clean heart in me, O God' and 'a contrite and humbled heart, O God, thou wilt not despise'. Allegri's setting was so prized that the Vatican forbade copies — until the fourteen-year-old Mozart wrote it out from memory.

t: 'He that dwelleth in the aid of the most High'
n: Psalm 90 (Hebrew 91): the psalm of protection, prayed at Compline every night. Satan quotes verses 11–12 to Jesus in the desert ('he hath given his angels charge over thee') — proof that the devil can quote Scripture.

Psalm 109 (Hebrew 110) is the psalm the New Testament quotes most. 'Sit thou at my right hand' — Jesus asks how David can call his own descendant 'Lord' (Matt 22:44). 'Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech' is the foundation of Hebrews' theology of Christ's priesthood.

Psalm 117 (Hebrew 118) was sung at Passover and on Palm Sunday: 'Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord'. Jesus applies the rejected stone to himself (Matt 21:42), and Peter to the resurrection (Acts 4:11). 'This is the day which the Lord hath made' is the Church's Easter refrain.

t: 'Thy word is a lamp to my feet'
n: Psalm 118 (Hebrew 119) is the longest chapter in the Bible: 176 verses in twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, every verse but one naming the Law. Monks divided it across the daytime hours; it is a love poem to God's word.

Psalm 129 (Hebrew 130): 'Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord'. The great psalm of penance and hope, prayed for the dead in the Catholic tradition and the source of Oscar Wilde's title. 'With the Lord there is mercy, and with him plentiful redemption.'

Psalm 136 (Hebrew 137): the exiles hang up their harps and refuse to sing for their captors. The psalm's last verse, blessing the one who dashes Babylon's infants against the rock, is one of the Bible's most disturbing lines — raw grief that the Church omits from public prayer but keeps in the book.

The Psalter ends in pure praise: trumpets, psaltery, harp, timbrel, strings, organs and cymbals. 'Let every spirit praise the Lord' — thirteen 'praise' in six verses. The five books of Psalms move from the lament of the individual to the praise of everything that breathes.

t: 'The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom'
n: Not terror but reverence — living as if God is real. This motto governs Proverbs, and Job 28, Psalm 110 and Sirach 1 repeat it. Proverbs collects sayings attributed to Solomon and others; its wisdom is practical, earthy and international, shared with Egypt and Mesopotamia.

Wisdom speaks as a person: 'The Lord possessed me in the beginning of his ways... I was with him forming all things'. Fourth-century Christians fought over whether the Vulgate's 'possessed' or the Greek 'created' applied to Christ; John's 'In the beginning was the Word' grows from this soil.

An acrostic poem — each verse starts with the next Hebrew letter — praising a woman who runs an estate, trades, gives to the poor, and 'shall laugh in the latter day'. Jewish husbands sing it to their wives on Friday nights. 'Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: the woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.'

Hebrew hevel — breath, vapour, mist. Ecclesiastes (Qoheleth, 'the Preacher') is the Bible's sceptic: work, pleasure, wisdom and wealth all pass; 'there is nothing new under the sun'. The rabbis nearly excluded it; it stayed because it ends with 'fear God and keep his commandments' and because it is true.

'A time to be born and a time to die... a time to weep and a time to laugh' — fourteen pairs. The passage became a folk song in the 1960s. Its point is not resignation but that no season is permanent, and that God 'hath made all things good in their time'.

A collection of love poems, frankly erotic, with no mention of God. Israel read it as the love between the Lord and his people; the Church as Christ and the Church, or Christ and the soul. Rabbi Akiva called it 'the holy of holies' of Scripture; Bernard of Clairvaux preached eighty-six sermons and only reached chapter 2.

The climax of the Song: love is a seal on the heart, 'its lamps are fire and flames', and 'many waters cannot quench' it. This is the closest the Old Testament comes to saying that love outlasts death — quoted at weddings and funerals alike.

t: The wicked plot against the just man
n: 'Let us examine him by outrages and tortures... let us condemn him to a most shameful death.' Written in Greek in Alexandria a century before Christ, this passage reads like a script of Good Friday; the Church reads it in Holy Week. Wisdom is deuterocanonical, absent from Jewish and Protestant Bibles.

t: 'The souls of the just are in the hand of God'
n: 'They seemed, in the eyes of the unwise, to die... but they are in peace.' The first clear Old Testament statement of immortality, written under Greek influence. It is the most common reading at Catholic funerals.

Written in Hebrew by Jesus ben Sirach in Jerusalem about 180 BC and translated into Greek by his grandson, this is the longest wisdom book. Its Latin name Ecclesiasticus, 'the church book', comes from how much the early Church used it for teaching converts. Hebrew fragments were found at Qumran and Masada.

t: 'Let us now praise men of renown'
n: A roll-call of Israel's heroes from Enoch to Nehemiah — Sirach's history of the world in portraits. James Agee borrowed the opening for his book on Alabama tenant farmers, turning the praise toward the unknown: 'and some there be which have no memorial'.

In the Temple, the year King Ozias died (about 740 BC), Isaias sees the Lord enthroned and the seraphim crying 'Holy, holy, holy' — the Sanctus sung at every Mass. His lips are cleansed with a coal, and he volunteers: 'Lo, here am I, send me'.

The most disputed verse between Jews and Christians. Hebrew almah means 'young woman'; the Greek Septuagint chose parthenos, 'virgin', and Matthew 1:23 quotes that. In context the sign concerns a child born in King Achaz's own day; Christians read a second, fuller meaning. Compare the JPS reading in this app.

'Wonderful, Counsellor, God the Mighty, the Father of the world to come, the Prince of Peace' — the names of a royal child, sung at Christmas since Handel. Originally an accession oracle for a king of Judah, perhaps Ezechias; the Church reads it at Midnight Mass.

t: The rod out of the root of Jesse
n: A shoot from a felled stump: the Davidic dynasty cut down but sprouting again. The seven gifts of the Spirit in Catholic teaching come from verses 2–3 (the Vulgate's 'piety' making the Hebrew six into seven). The wolf dwelling with the lamb is the Bible's picture of creation restored.

Chapter 40 opens the 'Book of Consolation' (Isaias 40–55), addressed to the exiles in Babylon a century and a half after the prophet of chapter 1 — most scholars speak of a 'Second Isaias'. 'The voice of one crying in the desert: prepare ye the way of the Lord' is applied by all four Gospels to John the Baptist.

The fourth 'Servant Song' begins here and runs through chapter 53. Who is the servant — Israel, the prophet, a future figure? Jews have mostly read Israel; Christians since Philip and the Ethiopian (Acts 8) have read Jesus. Read the JPS alongside the Vulgate to see how the ambiguity plays.

'Despised and the most abject of men, a man of sorrows... he was wounded for our iniquities... as a sheep before her shearers, he shall be dumb.' No Old Testament chapter is quoted more in the New Testament passion narratives. The servant suffers not for his own sins but for others' — the heart of the Christian reading of the cross.

t: 'The Spirit of the Lord is upon me'
n: The passage Jesus unrolled in the synagogue of Nazareth and then said, 'This day is fulfilled this scripture in your ears' (Luke 4:21). Good news to the poor, liberty to captives, the year of the Lord's favour — a jubilee proclamation.

'Before I formed thee in the bowels of thy mother, I knew thee.' Jeremias protests that he is a child; God touches his mouth. His forty-year ministry (627–586 BC) ends in the ruin he foretold, and he weeps through it — 'the weeping prophet'. He is the Old Testament figure most like Jesus in his suffering.

The only place the Old Testament uses the phrase: a covenant written 'in their heart', where 'all shall know me, from the least of them even to the greatest'. Hebrews 8 quotes the whole passage; Jesus' words 'the new testament in my blood' at the Last Supper point here.

t: 'The mercies of the Lord... are new every morning'
n: Lamentations is five poems over the burnt city of 586 BC, four of them alphabetical acrostics — grief given a form. At the exact centre of the book comes this turn to hope: 'his mercies are new every morning; great is thy faithfulness'. The Church sings Lamentations in the dark of Holy Week (Tenebrae).

Baruch, Jeremias' secretary, is placed after Lamentations in Catholic Bibles. Its poem on wisdom ends, in the Vulgate, 'afterwards he was seen upon earth, and conversed with men' (3:38) — read by the Fathers as a prophecy of the Incarnation. Chapter 6, the 'Letter of Jeremias', mocks idols.

Four living creatures with four faces (man, lion, ox, eagle), wheels within wheels full of eyes, and a throne above — God appears to the exiles beside a Babylonian canal, showing he is not confined to Jerusalem's Temple. The four faces became the symbols of the four evangelists; Jewish mysticism (merkavah) grew from this chapter.

'Son of man, dost thou think these bones shall live?' The bones knit, the flesh comes, and the breath (ruach — also 'wind' and 'spirit') enters them. Written for exiles who said 'our hope is lost', it is the Old Testament's clearest picture of national resurrection and, for Christians, of the resurrection of the body.

t: The song of the three young men
n: In the Vulgate, the three youths in the furnace sing a long canticle (verses 24–90) that the Hebrew Daniel lacks: 'All ye works of the Lord, bless the Lord' — the Benedicite, sung on Sundays and feasts in the Divine Office. The mysterious fourth figure in the fire, 'like the son of God', was read as Christ or an angel.

Coming 'with the clouds of heaven' to the Ancient of Days and receiving an everlasting kingdom. This is the source of Jesus' favourite title for himself, and of his answer to the high priest, 'you shall see the Son of man... coming in the clouds' (Mark 14:62), which sealed his condemnation.

Seventy 'weeks' of years until 'the Holy of holies may be anointed' and 'Christ shall be slain' (Vulgate). This dense prophecy has been calculated in every century — from the Maccabean crisis to the crucifixion to the end of the world. Its original horizon is the desecration of the Temple in 167 BC.

A young woman falsely accused of adultery by two elders who tried to seduce her; young Daniel cross-examines them separately and exposes the lie. Preserved only in Greek, it is chapter 13 in the Vulgate and 'apocryphal' in Protestant Bibles. Rembrandt and many others painted the bathing scene.

t: 'I called my son out of Egypt'
n: God as a father teaching a toddler to walk, lifting him to his cheek. Matthew 2:15 applies 'out of Egypt have I called my son' to the Holy Family's return. Osee's own marriage to an unfaithful wife (chapters 1–3) is the book's living parable of God's stubborn love for Israel.

t: 'I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh'
n: 'Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy... your young men shall see visions.' Peter's Pentecost sermon opens with this passage (Acts 2:17): the Spirit for everyone, not only prophets and kings. Vulgate numbering places these verses in chapter 2 (Hebrew Bibles begin chapter 3 here).

God rejects feasts, sacrifices and hymns from a people who cheat the poor: 'take away from me the tumult of thy songs'. Amos, a shepherd from Tecua sent to the prosperous northern kingdom, is the prophet of social justice; Martin Luther King quoted this verse in 'I have a dream'.

t: Jonas in the belly of the fish
n: Three days in the fish, and a psalm prayed from inside it. Jesus calls it the only sign he will give — 'as Jonas was in the whale's belly three days... so shall the Son of man be in the heart of the earth' (Matt 12:40). The book is a satire on a prophet who resents God's mercy toward Nineveh.

Out of the smallest clan of Judah 'shall come forth unto me he that is to be the ruler in Israel, and his going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity'. When Herod asks where the Christ is to be born, the scribes quote this verse (Matt 2:6).

t: 'What doth the Lord require of thee?'
n: 'To do judgment, and to love mercy, and to walk solicitous with thy God.' The prophets' summary of religion in one line, preferred to 'thousands of rams'. It appears on countless walls and became the motto of humanitarian movements.

t: 'The just shall live in his faith'
n: Habacuc complains that God tolerates evil; God answers that the vision will come and 'the just shall live in his faith'. Paul builds Romans and Galatians on this half-verse; Luther's reading of it began the Reformation. Hebrew emunah is closer to 'faithfulness' than to belief.

t: The king riding on a donkey
n: 'Rejoice greatly, O daughter of Sion... thy king will come to thee, the just and saviour: he is poor, and riding upon an ass.' Jesus stages his entry into Jerusalem on Palm Sunday to fulfil this verse (Matt 21:5). A king on a donkey, not a war-horse: peace, not conquest.

t: 'I will send you Elias the prophet'
n: The last words of the Old Testament in the Christian ordering: Elias will return before 'the great and dreadful day' to turn hearts of fathers to children. Luke 1:17 applies this to John the Baptist. Vulgate numbering: some Bibles place these verses at the end of chapter 3.

When a royal officer demands pagan sacrifice at Modin, the priest Mathathias kills him and the collaborator and flees to the hills with his sons — Judas Maccabeus among them. Written in Hebrew about 100 BC, 1 Maccabees is our main source for the revolt commemorated at Hanukkah (4:36–59).

t: The mother and her seven sons
n: Seven brothers tortured to death one after another for refusing pork, encouraged by their mother, each confessing hope in bodily resurrection: 'the King of the world will raise us up'. The clearest Old Testament statement of resurrection, and the model for the Christian martyr narratives.

t: 'It is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead'
n: Judas sends money to Jerusalem for a sacrifice on behalf of fallen soldiers found with pagan amulets. Catholic teaching on purgatory and prayer for the dead cites this verse; its absence from the Hebrew canon was one reason the Reformers set the book aside.
